title: What if…
lede: Three decisions where the story could have gone differently. The “What if” panels are speculation, labeled as such.

forks.tab: Sell it to the people who liked it
forks.actual: Coors aimed Zima at men, told stores to keep it away from the wine coolers and answered its popularity with women by launching Zima Gold for men in 1995. Gold was withdrawn the same year.[^12][^13][^3] Only in 2007 was the brand relaunched for women in their twenties.[^13]
forks.whatif: Accepting the audience it had in 1995 would have meant a smaller brand than the launch promised, but possibly a steadier one. The agency’s own advice at the time was not to chase the drinker who had rejected the product: “Let him have his Sam Adams.”[^12] In Japan, where the brand carried none of this baggage, it sold more than a million cases a year two decades later.[^29]

forks.actual: Zima went from a third of the country to national distribution in early 1994 behind an advertising push reported at $38 million to $50 million.[^1][^12][^13] Most drinkers tried it within the year, and the assistant brand manager later said the hype “totally fed into people not wanting to accept it.”[^12]
forks.whatif: A regional build over several years would have produced a lower peak and less of a collapse to explain to investors in 1995. It would also have given rivals time to launch their own clear malts first. Whether the taste would have held more drinkers at any speed is the open question.

forks.actual: MillerCoors ended production in October 2008, then found in 2017 that a limited summer run sold two-thirds of its stock in four weeks. It repeated the run once, in 2018, and stopped.[^14][^26][^28]
forks.whatif: An annual summer release might have kept the name in use in the United States at little cost. Instead the U.S. trademark registration was allowed to expire in 2024, leaving the name open to others.[^32] The hard seltzer boom of 2019 suggests the appetite for a clear, light, flavoured malt drink was there.[^35]
